Merge PDF Files

Combine multiple PDF files into one. Drag to reorder before merging. Everything stays in your browser — no upload, no signup.

📄
Drop PDF files here
or click to browse — add as many as you need

What actually happens when you merge PDFs here

Most online PDF mergers upload your files to a server, process them remotely, and send back the result. Aeroniqx does none of that. When you click Merge, your browser loads the pdf-lib JavaScript library and does all the work locally — reading each file's page structure, copying pages into a new PDF document, and writing the output file directly into your browser's memory. The merged PDF is never on any server. It goes from your disk → your browser tab → back to your disk.

This means merge speed depends on your device, not your internet connection. A 50-page document typically merges in 2–4 seconds on a modern laptop. On older phones it may take 10–15 seconds for large files. No spinning loading bar waiting for a server response.

Page order matters more than you think

The most common mistake people make is not checking page order before downloading. The file listed first becomes pages 1 onwards. If you're submitting a job application, your cover letter should be first — not your resume. If you're filing a loan application, the application form usually needs to precede supporting documents.

Use the ↑↓ arrows to arrange files before clicking Merge. Once you've downloaded the merged PDF, check the first and last pages to confirm the order is right before submitting anywhere important. Re-doing a merge takes 30 seconds — re-doing a submission because the pages were reversed costs much more.

Real situations where you need to merge PDFs

Job applications: Most applicant tracking systems accept one PDF. Merge your resume, cover letter, and certificates in that order — cover letter first if you want it read first, resume first if the recruiter is scanning quickly.

Government portal submissions: Portals like DigiLocker, UPSC DAF, and various state government portals frequently require supporting documents as a single combined PDF. They'll specify a file size limit too — merge first, then compress if needed using the PDF Compress tool.

Bank and loan documents: Salary slips, bank statements, ITR, and address proof combined into one PDF is the standard format most lenders expect. Merging them here keeps everything offline and private.

Client deliverables: Reports, proposals, and presentations assembled from multiple source files — merge the cover, body, and appendix into one final PDF before sending to clients.

What this tool cannot do — and what to use instead

Browser-based merging has real limitations worth knowing. Password-protected PDFs will fail — pdf-lib can't read encrypted files without the password. Unlock the PDF in Adobe Reader first (File → Properties → Security → Remove Password), then merge here.

Very large files (100MB+ per file) may cause the browser tab to run out of memory, especially on phones or older computers. For large files, PDF24's desktop app or Adobe Acrobat handles this better since they're not constrained by browser memory limits.

Merge with page reordering (interleaving pages from two documents) isn't supported here — this tool concatenates whole files. If you need to interleave pages (e.g. odd pages from file A + even pages from file B), use Adobe Acrobat or PDFsam Basic (free desktop software).

Frequently asked questions

Does merging change the PDF quality in any way?

No — and this is worth understanding clearly. pdf-lib merges PDFs by copying the raw page content objects from each source file into a new PDF container. It doesn't render pages, doesn't re-encode images, and doesn't touch fonts or vector graphics. The pages in the output are bit-for-bit identical to the source pages. If your source files are sharp, the merged output is sharp. If one source file has blurry scans, those blurry scans appear in the merged file exactly as they were.

Why is the merged file larger than the sum of the originals?

Sometimes merged PDFs are slightly larger than expected because pdf-lib doesn't deduplicate shared resources — if both source PDFs embed the same font, the merged file contains two copies of it. This is usually a small difference (a few KB for typical fonts). If final file size matters (for a portal upload limit), run the merged file through the PDF Compress tool afterwards.

How many files can I merge at once?

There's no hard limit set by the tool — you can add 20 files if you need to. The practical ceiling is your device's RAM. Each PDF is loaded into memory in full during the merge. A rough rule: if the total size of all your source files is under 200MB, you're unlikely to hit any issues on a modern device. Beyond that, results depend on your browser and available memory.

Can I merge a PDF with a scanned document?

Yes. From the tool's perspective, a scanned PDF and a text PDF are both just PDFs — they both get merged the same way. Scanned PDFs tend to be larger (since each page is an embedded image), so a merge involving several high-resolution scans may take longer and produce a larger output file. If you need to reduce the final file size, compress after merging.

Is this tool free forever?

Yes. There are no usage limits, no watermarks added to output files, no hidden caps after a certain number of merges, and no account required. The tool runs on open-source libraries (pdf-lib) in your browser, so there's no per-use server cost to pass on to you.
